messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcel, a 55‑year‑old fashion designer who has spent the last decade designing avant‑garde streetwear in Los Angeles, carries a quiet, palpable tension that colors every aspect of his life. When he was eight, his mother—who had been emotionally unstable—would lift his small frame and slam his head against the kitchen wall, shouting that he was “too loud” and “worth nothing.” The violence was not rare; it came daily, in bursts that left Marcel hollow and trembling, his small body shuddering with each impact. Even in the safety of his own home now, the echo of those blows lingers; he senses a danger in a stranger’s touch, in a sudden silence, and feels as if the world might collapse whenever a wall is closed or a phone rings. He tells his therapist that he sometimes wakes in the middle of the night, eyes wide, heart hammering, the dream images too vivid to name and too frightening to linger. The weight of that early violence has settled into Marcel’s self‑conception. He believes, with a grim certainty, that he has been permanently damaged and that he will never escape the suspicion that others harbor hidden malice. Those negative appraisals seep into his thoughts as he begins each day. He blames colleagues who ask him to finish a garment in a day he cannot meet, and he finds himself dwelling on the wrongs he has done—missing deadlines, refusing to speak up in meetings—while simultaneously accusing others of being untrustworthy. His rumination, both other‑blame and self‑blame, becomes a habitual way of coping; it keeps his mind occupied, preventing the intrusive dreams that haunt him from entering his conscious awareness. The more he believes he is irrevocably harmed, the more he feels the need to keep himself mentally and physically guarded, and the more he steers clear of any situation that might awaken his nightmares. When Marcel’s mind drifts toward memories of that childhood, the images are fragmented, devoid of a clear narrative. He can recall the bruise on his cheek, the cold breath of his mother, the sharp sting of a hammer—yet these details feel detached, almost foreign, as if they belong to someone else’s story. Each recollection is laced with a sudden surge of terror, a startle response that brings the same alarms he experiences during a quiet hallway. The memory of being hit becomes a catalyst for threat; the threat of another blow, of an invisible hand that could still strike, loops back into his mind and forces him to rehearse the past again. In turn, this reheating of images feeds the negative appraisal that he is doomed to repeat the violence or that he might go mad if he cannot control the sensations. The cycle tightens as the more he ruminates—both on his perceived failures and on others’ betrayals—the more fragmented and emotionally numb his recollections become. His avoidance of dreams is a conscious, maladaptive effort to block these memories, but it only makes the fragmented recollections more frequent, as his mind is left to assemble the broken pieces on its own. The constant threat that hovers over him—whether a stranger’s touch, an unexpected silence, or the hush of his own apartment—fuels his sense of being on edge, even when he is alone. This heightened sense of danger exacerbates his belief that he is going insane; he thinks that such hypervigilance is evidence of a mind unraveling. The feeling of mental instability, in turn, reinforces his negative appraisals, cementing the idea that he has become a dangerous, unstable person. As these thoughts spiral, the more he blames himself, the more he avoids even discussing his feelings with anyone, and the more he feels isolated in a world that appears hostile and untrustworthy. The loop is self‑reinforcing: negative appraisals give rise to maladaptive strategies, which in turn amplify memory fragmentation and threat perception, which feed back into the appraisals. Marcel has reached a point where the weight of his internal world feels like a physical burden on his shoulders. He can no longer ignore the mornings he wakes with his heart racing, his palms clammy, convinced that his house is being watched. He has begun to skip meetings with clients out of fear that their questions will trigger a flashback, and he has stopped showing his latest collection to colleagues because the idea of judgment feels like a potential assault. The isolation has cost him a friendship that had begun to bloom, and he has stopped painting in the studio for fear that the rhythm of a brush could trigger a memory. He recognizes that these behaviors are preventing him from living the life he once imagined, yet he cannot bring himself to confront them alone. It is the accumulation of sleepless nights, the growing sense of unreality, and the loss of meaningful connection that finally led him to seek help, hoping to break the tightening cycle and to regain a sense of safety in his own skin. He fears that he will never feel the ease of a quiet home again, but he also longs to reclaim the creative spark that once defined him.
